title: The skeleton and joints
blurb: Sort bones into axial and appendicular, count vertebrae and ribs, and match every joint type to its movement and example.
question: During a range-of-motion check, a patient turns her palm up, then swings her arm in a full circle at the shoulder. Which movements are these, and which joint types make them possible?

teach.body: Formally, the adult skeleton has 206 bones divided into the axial skeleton (80 bones along the body's central axis) and the appendicular skeleton (126 bones of the limbs and the girdles that attach them). In plain English: the axial skeleton is the trunk and head; the appendicular skeleton is everything that hangs off it. Infants have about 270 to 300 bones because many later fuse.

teach.caption: The girdles are appendicular: the clavicle and the hip bones are not axial.

head: Region
Number
Note
rows: 33 vertebrae at birth, 26 bones in adults
teach.caption: Normal curves: cervical and lumbar lordosis, thoracic and sacral kyphosis. Scoliosis is a lateral curve.
The radius is on the thumb side; the tibia bears the weight. The patella (kneecap) is a sesamoid bone.
Synovial joints have a capsule, synovial membrane and fluid (lubricates, nourishes cartilage), articular cartilage and ligaments.
Cartilage has no blood vessels, so it heals slowly.

teach.body: Jasmine, a nursing student, checks a patient's movement. Bending the elbow decreases the joint angle (flexion) at a hinge joint. Turning the palm up is supination, and palm down is pronation, made possible by the pivot joint between radius and ulna. Swinging the arm in a cone at the shoulder is circumduction, which needs a ball-and-socket joint. Lifting the arm sideways away from the midline is abduction; bringing it back is adduction.

teach.text: The knee is a HINGE, the hip a BALL-AND-SOCKET. Floating ribs are 11–12, not 8–10. Skull sutures are FIBROUS joints and intervertebral discs are FIBROCARTILAGE. The radius is lateral and the tibia bears weight. Supination is palm UP.

items: 206 bones: axial 80 (skull, hyoid, ossicles, spine, rib cage), appendicular 126 (girdles, limbs).
Vertebrae: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, sacrum, coccyx. Ribs: 1–7 true, 8–12 false, 11–12 floating.
Femur longest; patella sesamoid; calcaneus heel; hyoid touches no other bone.
Ball-and-socket: shoulder, hip. Hinge: elbow, knee. Pivot: C1–C2. Saddle: thumb.

summary: You can now sort bones into the axial and appendicular skeleton, recall vertebra and rib counts, and classify bones by shape. You can also match each joint class and synovial joint type to its movement and example, and name the body movements they allow.

A.q: Which bone belongs to the appendicular skeleton?
A.why: The clavicle is part of the pectoral girdle, which belongs to the appendicular skeleton.

whyNot.0: The sternum is part of the rib cage, in the axial skeleton.
whyNot.1: The hyoid is an axial bone in the neck.
whyNot.3: The sacrum is part of the vertebral column, in the axial skeleton.

A.q: Which numbers give the adult count of cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebrae, in that order?
A.why: There are 7 cervical, 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar vertebrae.

whyNot.1: Cervical and thoracic are swapped: the 12 thoracic vertebrae match the 12 pairs of ribs.
whyNot.2: Thoracic and lumbar are swapped: there are 12 thoracic and 5 lumbar.
whyNot.3: There are 7 cervical vertebrae, not 5, and 5 lumbar, not 7.

A.q: Which of these is a ball-and-socket joint?
A.why: The hip, like the shoulder, is a ball-and-socket joint allowing movement in all planes and rotation.

whyNot.0: The knee is a (modified) hinge joint.
whyNot.1: The elbow is a hinge joint.
whyNot.2: The wrist (radiocarpal) is a condyloid joint.

B.q: Which ribs are the floating ribs?
B.why: Rib pairs 11 and 12 are floating ribs: they have no anterior attachment.

whyNot.1: Pairs 1 to 7 are true ribs, each with its own costal cartilage to the sternum.
whyNot.2: Pairs 8 to 10 are false ribs attached through rib 7's cartilage, not floating.
whyNot.3: Pairs 8 to 12 are all false ribs, but only 11 and 12 float.

B.q: The patella is classified as which type of bone?
B.why: The patella develops inside the quadriceps tendon, so it is a sesamoid bone.

whyNot.0: Short bones are cube-like, such as the carpals and tarsals.
whyNot.2: Flat bones are thin and curved, such as the cranial bones and sternum.
whyNot.3: Irregular bones have complex shapes, such as the vertebrae.

B.q: Which joint is correctly matched to its structural class?
B.why: The pubic symphysis is a cartilaginous joint (a symphysis), usually slightly movable.

whyNot.0: Skull sutures are fibrous, immovable joints.
whyNot.1: The elbow is a synovial hinge joint.
whyNot.2: The first rib-sternum joint is cartilaginous (a synchondrosis) and immovable.

C.q: During a range-of-motion check, Jasmine asks a patient to turn his palm to face upward. Which movement is this, and at which joint type?
C.why: Turning the palm up is supination; it relies on the pivot joint between the radius and ulna (proximal radioulnar).

whyNot.1: Pronation turns the palm down, the opposite movement.
whyNot.2: The elbow hinge allows flexion and extension, not turning of the palm.
whyNot.3: Circumduction is a cone-shaped movement, and the saddle joint is at the base of the thumb.

C.q: Which statement about the skeleton is CORRECT?
options: The fibula is the main weight-bearing leg bone
The hyoid articulates directly with the mandible
The pelvic girdle is part of the axial skeleton
The radius is on the thumb side of the forearm
C.why: In anatomical position the radius is lateral, on the thumb side; the ulna is medial.

whyNot.0: The tibia is the larger, weight-bearing shin bone; the fibula bears little weight.
whyNot.1: The hyoid is the one bone that does not articulate with any other bone.
whyNot.2: The pelvic girdle (hip bones) is appendicular.

C.q: Intervertebral discs and knee menisci are made of which tissue, and why does it suit them?
options: Hyaline cartilage, which forms smooth joint surfaces
Elastic cartilage, which allows flexible recoil
Dense bone, which gives rigid support
C.why: Fibrocartilage is the strongest, shock-absorbing cartilage, ideal for discs, menisci and the pubic symphysis.

whyNot.1: Hyaline cartilage covers articular surfaces; discs are not hyaline.
whyNot.2: Elastic cartilage is found in the ear auricle and epiglottis.
whyNot.3: Discs and menisci are cartilage, which cushions; rigid bone could not absorb shock.

reteach.title: Joints as hardware
reteach.question: Walk around a house and look at its hardware: door hinges, a joystick, a doorknob, sliding drawers. Which body joint works like each one?

blocks.body: A door hinge swings one way and back: your elbow and knee. A joystick tilts in every direction and twists: your shoulder and hip, the ball-and-socket joints. A doorknob only turns: the pivot between atlas and axis when you shake your head 'no'. Drawers slide past each other: the plane joints between carpals. A rider sitting on a saddle can rock two ways: the thumb's base.

blocks.text: The knee feels like it should twist, but it is a hinge. The hip is the joystick.

explain.body: Axial (80): skull, hyoid, ear ossicles, vertebral column and rib cage. Appendicular (126): pectoral girdles (clavicle, scapula), upper limbs, pelvic girdle (hip bones) and lower limbs. The mandible is the only movable skull bone.

test.q: Which structure is part of the axial skeleton?
test.why: The sternum is part of the rib cage, which is axial.

whyNot.0: The scapula is part of the pectoral girdle, which is appendicular.
whyNot.1: The hip bones form the pelvic girdle, which is appendicular.
whyNot.3: The clavicle is part of the pectoral girdle, which is appendicular.

explain.body: 7 cervical vertebrae (C1 atlas holds the skull for nodding; C2 axis has the dens for rotation), 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, the sacrum (5 fused) and coccyx. 12 pairs of ribs: 1–7 true, 8–12 false, 11–12 floating.

test.q: Which vertebra allows the head to rotate from side to side, as in shaking the head 'no'?
test.why: The axis (C2) has the dens, around which the atlas pivots to rotate the head.

whyNot.0: The atlas (C1) holds the skull and allows the 'yes' nodding movement.
whyNot.2: The seventh cervical vertebra is not the rotation pivot for the head.
whyNot.3: The first thoracic vertebra articulates with ribs, far below the head's pivot.

explain.body: Upper limb: humerus, radius (lateral) and ulna (medial; olecranon is the point of the elbow), 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges. Lower limb: femur, patella, tibia (medial, weight-bearing) and fibula (lateral), 7 tarsals (talus meets the tibia; calcaneus is the heel), 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges.

test.why: The calcaneus is the heel bone, the largest tarsal.

whyNot.0: The talus is the tarsal that articulates with the tibia at the ankle.
whyNot.1: The tibia is the weight-bearing shin bone above the ankle.
whyNot.3: The metatarsals form the middle of the foot, not the heel.

explain.body: Flexion decreases a joint angle; extension increases it. Abduction moves away from the midline; adduction toward it. Circumduction is a cone (shoulder, hip). Supination turns the palm up, pronation down. Dorsiflexion lifts the toes; plantar flexion points them.

test.q: Raising the arm sideways, away from the body's midline, is called what?
test.why: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline.

whyNot.0: Adduction moves a limb toward the midline, the opposite direction.
whyNot.2: Circumduction moves the limb in a cone shape, not straight out to the side.
whyNot.3: Rotation turns a bone around its own long axis.
